reference.source: WHO Classification of Tumours: Thoracic Tumours
clinicalPearls: The commonest primary lung malignancy of early childhood, a dysembryonic mesenchymal tumour of lung and pleura, distinct from the epithelial pulmonary blastoma of adults.
Classified into three progressive types: Type I is purely cystic, Type II is mixed cystic and solid, and Type III is purely solid, with prognosis worsening across the sequence.
Type I may regress or, if untreated, progress to the aggressive Type II and III forms, so complete resection of Type I lesions is advocated.
Around two-thirds of cases arise in DICER1 syndrome; identifying a germline DICER1 pathogenic variant unlocks family surveillance.
It is frequently and dangerously mistaken for a benign congenital pulmonary airway malformation (CPAM) on imaging.
Presentations include respiratory distress, persistent cough, chest pain, and spontaneous pneumothorax.
The solid types metastasise with a particular predilection for the brain and bone.
DICER1 syndrome also predisposes to cystic nephroma, Sertoli-Leydig cell tumour, multinodular goitre, ciliary body medulloepithelioma, and nasal chondromesenchymal hamartoma.
reference.pathophysiology: Pleuropulmonary blastoma is a dysontogenetic tumour arising from the primitive mesenchyme of the developing lung and pleura. Most cases are associated with germline loss-of-function mutation in DICER1, an endoribonuclease essential for microRNA maturation; a characteristic somatic hotspot missense mutation in the RNase IIIb domain of the remaining allele deregulates microRNA processing and drives tumour formation. Disease begins as an epithelium-lined cystic lesion (Type I) harbouring a subtle malignant mesenchymal (cambium) layer beneath a benign-appearing epithelium; over time the mesenchyme overgrows to produce mixed (Type II) and then wholly solid, high-grade sarcomatous (Type III) tumours, which may display blastematous, rhabdomyosarcomatous, chondroid, and anaplastic elements.
additionalDifferentials: Bronchogenic or other foregut duplication cyst
Bronchopulmonary infection with cavitation or empyema
Metastatic sarcoma or Wilms tumour to the lung
additionalInvestigations: Contrast-enhanced CT of the chest to characterise cystic versus solid components
Histopathology of the resected lesion with attention to the malignant cambium layer
Germline and tumour DICER1 mutation testing
Brain MRI to screen for cerebral metastases in solid types
Echocardiography if there is mediastinal or cardiac displacement
Thyroid ultrasound and abdominal/pelvic imaging for DICER1-associated tumours
redFlags: Spontaneous pneumothorax in a young child, which may herald an underlying cystic pleuropulmonary blastoma
A presumed CPAM with solid components, septal thickening, or rapid enlargement
A family history of DICER1-associated tumours
reference.prognosis: Type I disease that is completely resected has a favourable outcome, whereas Type II and especially Type III tumours carry a substantially worse prognosis with significant risk of recurrence and metastatic spread; cerebral metastases are a particularly poor prognostic feature.
pitfalls: Diagnosing a cystic lung lesion as benign CPAM without histological review, missing an early Type I pleuropulmonary blastoma.
Adopting watchful waiting for complex cystic lung lesions in a child with a DICER1 background rather than resecting.
Not sending DICER1 testing, missing the syndrome and surveillance opportunities for the child and relatives.
Omitting brain imaging in solid-type disease and thereby missing metastases.
references: WHO Classification of Tumours: Thoracic Tumours
International Pleuropulmonary Blastoma / DICER1 Registry guidance
management: Perform complete surgical resection as the cornerstone of treatment, including excision of purely cystic Type I lesions to pre-empt progression to solid, higher-grade forms
Give adjuvant multi-agent sarcoma-type chemotherapy, such as combinations of vincristine, actinomycin, doxorubicin, cyclophosphamide and ifosfamide, for Type II and Type III disease
Consider radiotherapy for selected residual, unresectable or metastatic disease
Undertake germline and tumour DICER1 mutation testing, with genetic counselling and family surveillance when a pathogenic variant is found
Screen for and manage metastatic spread, including brain MRI for cerebral metastases and skeletal imaging
Manage acute complications such as pneumothorax and respiratory distress, and stabilise the airway when needed
Coordinate care through a paediatric oncology multidisciplinary team with long-term follow-up for recurrence and other DICER1-related tumours
